Below is a research plan that you can implement with your data as described. I propose a design that produces complementary causal parameters: (i) short-run local labor-market effects within regions and (ii) national skill-group effects that abstract from internal migration. I explicitly incorporate immigrant occupational downgrading into the treatment to reconcile divergent findings across the literature.

1. Identification Strategy
- Primary strategy: Shift-share IV within a generalized DID framework at the region-by-skill-by-year level (event-study for dynamics).
  - Use panel variation in immigrant inflows to region-skill cells over time (US commuting zones, UK TTWAs, German districts), with rich fixed effects.
  - Instrument the immigrant share in a cell using a leave-one-out shift-share (Bartik) instrument based on pre-period (baseline) origin-by-region settlement patterns and national-by-time inflows of immigrant origin groups, interacted with national-by-time skill (or occupation-task) distribution to capture downgrading.
  - Event-study estimates assess pre-trends and dynamic responses.
- Secondary strategy: National skill-cell IV panel (education-by-experience-by-year).
  - Use national-level variation in immigrant inflows to education-experience cells over time to estimate substitution elasticities within effective skill groups; instrument using a national origin-level inflow shock interacted with pre-period origin composition by skill (leave-one-out at the cell level).
- Why this is appropriate:
  - The regional design targets local wage/employment impacts allowing for native mobility and local adjustments—precisely the margin underlying “spatial” studies.
  - The national skill-cell design targets substitution within skill groups without contamination from native geographic re-sorting—precisely the margin of “national skill-cell” studies.
  - Modeling “effective” immigrant supply by weighting recent immigrants by their realized occupation/task placement (downgrading) aligns treatment with the margin of actual competition faced by natives.

2. Treatment and Control
- Unit of observation:
  - Primary: region-by-education-by-experience-by-year cells (r × s × t). Define education categories (e.g., low/mid/high) and experience bands (e.g., 0–9, 10–19, 20–29, 30–39).
  - Secondary: national education-by-experience-by-year cells (s × t).
- Treatment variable:
  - Effective immigrant share in cell c = (Imm_recent_effective + Imm_settled)/Employment_c, where:
    - Imm_recent_effective = sum over immigrants with years-since-migration ≤ 5 working in occupation/task group g of the cell, possibly below their education-based skill; operationalize with weights that map education-experience to occupation/task using observed distributions of recent immigrants.
    - Imm_settled = immigrants with YSM > 5, weighted ≈ 1 (less downgrading).
  - Practically: construct ImmShare_effective_c,t as the share of total hours or headcount in the cell accounted for by immigrants, where recent immigrants are counted in the cell of their observed occupation/task group and settled immigrants by their education-experience.
- Control group:
  - Cells with low or no exposure to immigrant inflows over the sample horizon. Identification uses within-country comparisons across cells after partialing out region, skill, and time effects.
- Treatment timing:
  - Continuous treatment that varies annually by cell. For event studies, define each cell’s “treatment start” as the first year its predicted effective immigrant share increases by at least 1 percentage point over baseline.
- Running variable and cutoff: Not applicable.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
- For IV (exclusion restriction):
  - Conditional on fixed effects and controls, national-by-origin inflow shocks shift local (or skill-cell) immigrant supply only through immigrant location decisions driven by pre-existing networks, not through local demand shocks that differentially affect high- vs. low-exposure cells.
  - Plausibility: In advanced economies, immigrant location strongly follows historical co-ethnic networks; leave-one-out and rich FE help purge local shocks. We further reduce confounding by interacting national inflows with pre-period skill/occupation distributions to separate “who arrives in which task” from local demand shifts.
- First-stage relevance:
  - Baseline origin-by-region and origin-by-skill shares predict subsequent immigrant settlement and task placement due to network effects and credential portability constraints (downgrading). Strong in practice.
- Parallel trends (for DID/event study):
  - In the absence of immigration shocks, high- and low-exposure cells would have evolved similarly after conditioning on region FE, skill FE, year FE, and region-specific trends. Plausible over 1995–2005 in the UK with rich controls; more tenuous cross-sectionally (Germany), hence the IV cross-section only there.
- Stable mapping/weighting for downgrading:
  - The occupation/task distribution of recent immigrants by education-experience evolves smoothly at the national level and is not driven by local shocks. We estimate weights from national distributions and conduct robustness with alternative definitions and time windows.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
- Endogenous immigrant placement to booming cells:
  - Mitigation: Use leave-one-out shift-share (exclude region r’s contribution when forming national shocks); include region FE, skill FE, year FE, and region-specific linear trends; control for observable local shocks (e.g., industry mix × global industry trends); drop large-origin contributors for robustness (e.g., Mexico in US, Poland in UK).
- Native mobility and composition changes:
  - Mitigation: Complement regional design with national skill-cell design; in regional regressions, examine outcomes for stayers (when possible), track native in-/out-migration as an outcome, and reweight or control for changing native composition (age-sex-education-experience within cells).
- Shift-share mechanical bias or common global shocks by origin:
  - Mitigation: Residualize national origin inflows on origin-by-year global demand proxies; use “many small shocks” diagnostics; drop top-k origin groups; cluster SEs two-way (region, origin) or use AKM-style SEs for shift-share.

5. R Code Outline
Assumptions:
- You have an individual-level CSV “micro.csv” with variables:
  - country, year, region, nativity (0/1), wage (log), employed (0/1), hours, educ_cat, exp_band, occ_group, ysm (years since migration), origin (country/region of birth), weight.
- We aggregate to region-skill-year cells and build instruments. The code uses fixest.

```r
# Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)

# 1) Load micro data
micro <- fread("micro.csv")

# Keep main countries and sample years
micro <- micro %>%
  filter(country %in% c("US","UK","DE")) %>%
  mutate(s = paste0(educ_cat, "_", exp_band)) # skill cell id

# Define "recent" immigrants and "settled"
micro <- micro %>%
  mutate(immigrant = as.integer(nativity == 1),
         recent = as.integer(immigrant == 1 & ysm <= 5),
         settled = as.integer(immigrant == 1 & ysm > 5))

# (Optional) Build hours; fallback to 1 if missing
micro$hrs <- ifelse(is.na(micro$hours), 1, micro$hours)

# Define outcome samples: natives only
micro <- micro %>%
  mutate(native = as.integer(nativity == 0))

# 2) Construct effective immigrant exposure with downgrading
# - Recent immigrants are assigned to occ_group cells (task-based),
#   settled immigrants to education-experience cells

# First, weight matrix for downgrading: national distribution of recent immigrants across occ_group by (educ,exp)
# Compute at country-year level to allow slow-moving change; then average across years as baseline
downg_w <- micro %>%
  filter(recent == 1) %>%
  group_by(country, year, educ_cat, exp_band, occ_group) %>%
  summarise(imm_rec_hrs = sum(hrs * weight, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") %>%
  group_by(country, year, educ_cat, exp_band) %>%
  mutate(w_occ = imm_rec_hrs / sum(imm_rec_hrs)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(country, educ_cat, exp_band, occ_group) %>%
  summarise(w_occ = mean(w_occ, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") %>%
  mutate(s = paste0(educ_cat,"_",exp_band))

# 3) Aggregate to region-skill-year cells
# Recent immigrants reassigned by occ_group weights into skill cells:
# For each region r, year t, skill s: Imm_recent_effective = sum over occ_group of Imm_recent_in_occ * w_occ(s, occ)
imm_recent_occ <- micro %>%
  filter(recent == 1) %>%
  group_by(country, year, region, occ_group) %>%
  summarise(imm_rec_hrs_occ = sum(hrs * weight, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop")

# Merge weights and spread recent immigrants into skill cells
imm_recent_eff <- downg_w %>%
  left_join(imm_recent_occ, by=c("country","occ_group")) %>%
  # Align years by merging the year dimension from imm_recent_occ; weights are country-level averages
  group_by(country, year, region, s) %>%
  summarise(imm_rec_eff_hrs = sum(imm_rec_hrs_occ * w_occ, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop")

# Settled immigrants kept by skill cell
imm_settled <- micro %>%
  filter(settled == 1) %>%
  group_by(country, year, region, s) %>%
  summarise(imm_sett_hrs = sum(hrs * weight, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop")

# Native hours and outcomes by cell
cells <- micro %>%
  filter(native == 1) %>%
  group_by(country, year, region, s) %>%
  summarise(
    nat_hrs = sum(hrs * weight, na.rm=TRUE),
    nat_emp = sum(employed * weight, na.rm=TRUE),
    nat_n = sum(weight, na.rm=TRUE),
    lwage = weighted.mean(wage, w=weight, na.rm=TRUE),
    .groups="drop"
  )

# Combine components
panel <- cells %>%
  full_join(imm_recent_eff, by=c("country","year","region","s")) %>%
  full_join(imm_settled,    by=c("country","year","region","s")) %>%
  mutate(across(c(imm_rec_eff_hrs, imm_sett_hrs, nat_hrs), ~replace_na(.,0)),
         tot_hrs = nat_hrs + imm_rec_eff_hrs + imm_sett_hrs,
         imm_eff_share = (imm_rec_eff_hrs + imm_sett_hrs) / pmax(tot_hrs, 1))

# 4) Build leave-one-out shift-share instrument
# Baseline year for shares
base_year_by_cty <- panel %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(base_year = min(year, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop")

# Baseline origin-region shares for recent immigrants (network shares), by country
base_shares <- micro %>%
  inner_join(base_year_by_cty, by="country") %>%
  filter(year == base_year, immigrant == 1) %>%
  group_by(country, region, origin) %>%
  summarise(imm_origin_reg = sum(weight, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") %>%
  group_by(country, region) %>%
  mutate(s_ro = imm_origin_reg / sum(imm_origin_reg, na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup()

# National-by-time inflows of immigrants by origin and skill (effective) EXCLUDING region r (leave-one-out)
# First, national counts of recent immigrants by origin, occ, year; merge weights to map to skill s
nat_recent_occ <- micro %>%
  filter(recent == 1) %>%
  group_by(country, year, origin, region, occ_group) %>%
  summarise(imm_rec_hrs_occ = sum(hrs * weight, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop")

# Map to skill using weights and then aggregate, then subtract region r later
nat_recent_skill <- downg_w %>%
  left_join(nat_recent_occ, by=c("country","occ_group")) %>%
  mutate(s = paste0(educ_cat,"_",exp_band)) %>%
  group_by(country, year, origin, region, s) %>%
  summarise(imm_rec_eff_hrs = sum(imm_rec_hrs_occ * w_occ, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop")

# Settled by skill (no downgrading needed)
nat_sett_skill <- micro %>%
  filter(settled == 1) %>%
  group_by(country, year, origin, region, s) %>%
  summarise(imm_sett_hrs = sum(hrs * weight, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop")

nat_skill <- full_join(nat_recent_skill, nat_sett_skill,
                       by=c("country","year","origin","region","s")) %>%
  mutate(across(c(imm_rec_eff_hrs, imm_sett_hrs), ~replace_na(.,0))) %>%
  group_by(country, year, origin, region, s) %>%
  summarise(imm_eff_hrs = sum(imm_rec_eff_hrs + imm_sett_hrs), .groups="drop")

# For each region r, compute leave-one-out national inflow by origin x skill
nat_skill_total <- nat_skill %>%
  group_by(country, year, origin, s) %>%
  summarise(national_imm_eff_hrs = sum(imm_eff_hrs, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop")

# merge instrument components
# predicted_imm_eff_{r,s,t} = sum_o s_ro^{base} * (national_imm_eff_{o,s,t} - imm_eff_{o,s,t in region r})
nat_skill_lo <- nat_skill %>%
  left_join(nat_skill_total, by=c("country","year","origin","s")) %>%
  mutate(nat_minus_r = pmax(national_imm_eff_hrs - imm_eff_hrs, 0)) %>%
  select(country, year, origin, region, s, nat_minus_r)

# Now compute instrument by summing across origins with base region-origin shares
instr <- base_shares %>%
  # expand over years and skills
  crossing(panel %>% distinct(country, year, s)) %>%
  left_join(nat_skill_lo, by=c("country","year","origin","region","s")) %>%
  group_by(country, year, region, s) %>%
  summarise(pred_imm_eff_hrs = sum(s_ro * nat_minus_r, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop")

# Scale to a share using baseline native hours (so denominator is pre-determined)
base_native <- panel %>%
  inner_join(base_year_by_cty, by="country") %>%
  filter(year == base_year) %>%
  select(country, region, s, nat_hrs) %>%
  rename(base_nat_hrs = nat_hrs)

panel <- panel %>%
  left_join(instr, by=c("country","year","region","s")) %>%
  left_join(base_native, by=c("country","region","s")) %>%
  mutate(base_nat_hrs = ifelse(is.na(base_nat_hrs) | base_nat_hrs <= 0, NA, base_nat_hrs),
         Z_pred_share = pred_imm_eff_hrs / base_nat_hrs)

# 5) Main IV specification (regional skill cells)
# Outcome 1: native log wage
# Fixed effects: region, skill, year; add region-specific trends as robustness

panel_est <- panel %>%
  filter(!is.na(lwage), !is.na(imm_eff_share), !is.na(Z_pred_share))

# Main IV
iv_wage <- feols(
  lwage ~ 1 | imm_eff_share ~ Z_pred_share | region + s + year,
  data = panel_est,
  cluster = ~ region
)
summary(iv_wage)

# Outcome 2: native employment rate in cell
panel_est <- panel_est %>%
  mutate(emp_rate = nat_emp / pmax(nat_n, 1))
iv_emp <- feols(
  emp_rate ~ 1 | imm_eff_share ~ Z_pred_share | region + s + year,
  data = panel_est,
  cluster = ~ region
)
summary(iv_emp)

# 6) Robustness check: region-specific linear trends
iv_wage_trend <- feols(
  lwage ~ 1 | imm_eff_share ~ Z_pred_share | region + s + year + i(region, year),
  data = panel_est,
  cluster = ~ region
)
summary(iv_wage_trend)

# 7) Robustness check: drop top-3 origin groups by baseline national share
top3 <- micro %>%
  group_by(country, origin) %>%
  summarise(baseline = sum(weight*(year==min(year)), na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  slice_max(order_by = baseline, n=3, with_ties=FALSE)

micro2 <- anti_join(micro, top3, by=c("country","origin"))
# (Re-run the aggregation and instrument steps on micro2 as above; omitted for brevity)
```

Notes:
- For the UK panel (1995–2005), this setup supports event studies by coding “treatment start” per cell as the first year Z_pred_share exceeds baseline + 1pp and using sunab() in fixest. For brevity, the above shows a static IV with rich FE and region-specific trends.
- For the national skill-cell IV design, repeat the above at the national s × t level, using origin-by-skill baseline shares and national inflows by origin over time; no region dimension or controls for internal migration needed.

6. Expected Results
- Within effective skill groups most directly exposed to recent immigrants (post-downgrading), I expect small negative effects on native wages and employment in the short run:
  - Wage elasticity with respect to the immigrant-induced effective labor supply in the range −0.1 to −0.3 for the most exposed native groups (e.g., low- to mid-education with 0–19 years experience).
  - Employment rate impacts small and negative in exposed cells, e.g., −0.05 to −0.15 elasticity.
- Aggregating across all natives or using broader definitions that do not account for downgrading, effects attenuate toward zero because:
  - Many immigrants are not close substitutes for same-education natives due to task mismatch.
  - Complementarities and task reallocation (especially for high-skill natives) offset substitution.
- Dynamics: Effects largest upon arrival (ysm ≤ 5) and fade as immigrants upskill/reclassify into higher-occupational tasks (downgrading dissipates).

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV-DID/event study)
- C1: Strong first stage (relevance of network-based shift-share): 1
- C2: Exclusion restriction (leave-one-out, rich FE, drop big origins): 0.7 (not perfect; origin shocks can correlate with local industry shocks)
- C3: Parallel trends/pre-trends (event-study evidence in UK; region trends): 0.8 (good with trends; weaker where only few years)
- C4: SUTVA/no spillovers across cells: 0.6 (some spillovers across neighboring regions and skills likely)
- C5: Stable downgrading weights/not driven by local shocks: 0.8 (national weighting and robustness across definitions help)

Why studies diverge under this framework:
- Unit of analysis matters: regional designs find small effects due to native mobility; national skill-cell designs sometimes find larger substitution effects. Not accounting for downgrading overstates competition between immigrants and highly educated natives. Our “effective exposure” reconciles these by aligning treatment with realized tasks, while two complementary designs separately identify local versus national-skill effects.
